hints: Remember what three products all Group 2 nitrates give on heating: a metal oxide, nitrogen dioxide and oxygen.
walkthrough:
Recall the standard Group 2 pattern**
Think of any Group 2 nitrate, from magnesium to barium. Heating never gives the metal alone. It always splits the nitrate ion to leave the oxide ion in the solid, while the rest leaves as two gases, brown $\text{NO}_2$ and $\text{O}_2$. So for strontium you must get $\text{SrO}$, $\text{NO}_2$ and $\text{O}_2$.

Balance the atoms**
Start with $\text{Sr(NO}_3\text{)}_2$. You have 1 Sr, 2 N and 6 O. To balance N you need $2\text{NO}_2$. That uses 4 O, leaving 2 O. One stays in $\text{SrO}$, the other one atom is $\frac{1}{2}\text{O}_2$. That gives $\text{Sr(NO}_3\text{)}_2 \rightarrow \text{SrO} + 2\text{NO}_2 + \frac{1}{2}\text{O}_2$.

hints: Decide first whether a larger cation at the bottom of the group makes the nitrate easier or harder to decompose on heating.
Think how ionic radius of the $\text{M}^{2+}$ ion changes from $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ to $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ and what that does to charge density.
Link high charge density to distortion of the $\text{NO}_3^-$ electron cloud and weakening of the N-O bond.
walkthrough:
State the observed trend**
Picture heating $\text{Mg(NO}_3\text{)}_2$ and $\text{Ba(NO}_3\text{)}_2$. Magnesium nitrate decomposes very easily at low temperature, barium nitrate needs much stronger heating. So stability increases going down the group as atomic number increases.

Follow the size of the cation**
All the cations are 2+, but $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ is tiny and $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ is large because extra electron shells are added down the group. Same charge spread over a larger volume means charge density falls from top to bottom.

See how the cation attacks the nitrate**
A small, highly charging $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ pulls strongly on the electrons of the nearby $\text{NO}_3^-$ ion. This polarisation distorts the nitrate ion and weakens an N-O bond, making it easy to break to give $\text{NO}_2$ and $\text{O}^{2-}$. A large $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ polarises much less, the nitrate stays more stable, so decomposition temperature rises.

Final answer: Thermal stability increases down Group 2 with increasing atomic number.
Down the group cationic radius increases / ion size increases.
Larger cation causes less polarisation / distortion of the $\text{NO}_3^-$ ion, so N-O bond is less weakened and more heat is needed to decompose.

hints: Use the same stability rule as for nitrates and compare the positions of calcium and barium in Group 2.
walkthrough:
Transfer the nitrate logic to amides**
You are told amides behave like nitrates. That means a smaller, more polarising cation gives a less stable compound. Calcium is above barium in Group 2, so $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ is smaller than $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ with higher charge density.

Make the prediction**
Because $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ distorts the $\text{NH}_2^-$ ion more strongly, $\text{Ca(NH}_2\text{)}_2$ is less thermally stable. It will therefore decompose more readily than $\text{Ba(NH}_2\text{)}_2$.
Final answer: More readily, because $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ has a smaller ionic radius / greater charge density than $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ and polarises the amide ion more.

hints: Write down the two products $\text{Ba}_3\text{N}_2$ and $\text{NH}_3$ and work out how many $\text{Ba(NH}_2\text{)}_2$ units you need to supply 3 Ba atoms.
walkthrough:
Match barium first**
The product $\text{Ba}_3\text{N}_2$ contains 3 Ba, so you must start with 3 $\text{Ba(NH}_2\text{)}_2$. That gives you 3 Ba, 6 N and 12 H on the left.

Balance N and H with ammonia**
$\text{Ba}_3\text{N}_2$ uses 2 of the 6 N, leaving 4 N to form ammonia. Each $\text{NH}_3$ needs 3 H, and $4 \times 3 = 12$ H which exactly matches the 12 H on the left. So $3\text{Ba(NH}_2\text{)}_2 \rightarrow \text{Ba}_3\text{N}_2 + 4\text{NH}_3$ balances perfectly.

hints: Count valence electrons on N in $\text{NH}_2^-$ to find the total number of electron pairs around N.
Split that total into bonding pairs to H and lone pairs left on N.
Recall the repulsion order lone pair-lone pair > lone pair-bond pair > bond pair-bond pair and how it squeezes the tetrahedral angle.
walkthrough:
Count electron pairs on nitrogen**
N is in Group 15 with 5 valence electrons. In $\text{NH}_2^-$ it forms 2 N-H bonds and gains one extra electron from the 1- charge. That gives $5 + 2 + 1 = 8$ electrons, or 4 pairs around N.

Work out the shape**
Two of those pairs are bonding pairs to the two H atoms, the other two are lone pairs. Four pairs would ideally point to the corners of a tetrahedron at $109.5^{\circ}$, but with only two atoms attached the molecular shape is bent, similar to water.

Apply lone pair repulsion**
Remember lone pairs are held closer to N and spread out more, so they push harder than bonding pairs. The order is lone pair-lone pair > lone pair-bond pair > bond pair-bond pair. The two lone pairs squeeze the two N-H bonds together, closing the H-N-H angle from $109.5^{\circ}$ down to about $104-105^{\circ}$.

Final answer: bond angle $104-105^{\circ}$
$\text{NH}_2^-$ has 2 bonding pairs and 2 lone pairs around N.
Lone pairs repel more strongly than bonding pairs, reducing the angle from $109.5^{\circ}$.
